query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In solidified Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloys, the dynamic mechanical response is governed by a temperature‐ and strain‐rate–dependent evolution of localized deformation bands that arise from the cooperative interplay between dislocation glide and deformation twinning. At lower strain rates and higher temperatures, deformation is dominated by dislocation slip, whereas at higher strain rates (and/or lower temperatures) increased twin nucleation and interaction lead to the formation of dense shear-localized bands that enhance work hardening and delay catastrophic localization.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenous, solidified Co–free FeNiCrMn alloy with a primarily FCC structure and minimal preexisting defects.
generation.intervention: Conduct controlled mechanical tests (compression and/or tension) over a wide range of strain rates (from quasi-static ~10^−3 s^−1 to dynamic >10^3 s^−1) and temperatures (from cryogenic to ambient) using in situ techniques (e.g., SEM/DIC and TEM) to monitor local strain fields and defect evolution.
generation.conditions: Ambient to cryogenic temperatures with strain rates varying from ~10^−3 s^−1 under quasi-static loading up to >10^3 s^−1 in dynamic experiments; tests performed on solidified samples with uniform microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and evolution of localized deformation bands enriched in dislocation structures and deformation twins.
generation.mechanism: The mechanism involves a shift in the dominant deformation mode: at low strain rates/high temperatures, plasticity is primarily accommodated by dislocation motion, while at high strain rates/low temperatures the increased stress promotes twinning, which leads to the development of dense deformation bands. These bands act as internal barriers that enhance strain hardening, thereby preserving the strength–ductility balance even under dynamic conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Testing will reveal a systematic transition: at higher strain rates (or lower temperatures) an increase in twinning and deformation band density will directly correlate with enhanced work hardening and higher dynamic yield strength without compromising ductility. The stress–strain curves will display a shift from smoothly increasing slopes under quasi-static conditions to marked serration and higher flow stress under dynamic loading.
generation.baseline: Under quasi-static loading at room temperature, where dislocation slip predominates and only minor twin formation is observed, resulting in the standard work-hardening behavior of the alloy.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to solidified, Co–free FeNiCrMn alloys with a mainly FCC structure. It may not extend to samples with significant phase segregation, multiphase microstructures, or those processed through methods that intentionally introduce heterogeneity prior to testing. Extremely high strain rates causing catastrophic thermal softening (e.g., severe adiabatic shear) are beyond the regime where this mechanism is expected to govern behavior.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds on observations of serration behavior and deformation band evolution in related high-entropy alloys (e.g., evidence from PMC7512474 and PMC7846165) together with reports on twinning-induced plasticity in dynamic regimes (PMC7012927, PMC5701024). What is new is the attribution of these effects specifically to the Co-free FeNiCrMn system. Uncertainties remain regarding the exact critical defect density required for the transition and whether the stacking fault energy in FeNiCrMn is sufficiently low to favor twinning to the same degree as in alloys containing Co.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of homogeneous, solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy specimens with minimal initial defects. Perform a controlled series of uniaxial compression or tensile tests across a matrix of strain rates (from ~10^−3 s^−1 to >10^3 s^−1) and temperatures (from cryogenic to ambient). Use in situ high-resolution imaging (such as SEM combined with digital image correlation and TEM for selected tests) to quantitatively map local deformation features (dislocation density, twin formation, deformation bands).
measurements: Stress–strain curves and work hardening rates
Quantitative density of dislocations versus twins from microstructural imaging
Spatial maps of localized deformation bands
Correlation of yield strength and ductility with testing conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental results do not show a systematic increase in deformation twinning and the formation of localized deformation bands (i.e., if dislocation slip remains the dominant mechanism at high strain rates or low temperatures) and no corresponding enhancement in strain hardening or yield strength is observed relative to quasi-static behavior, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Figure 4a,b show a strength-ductility index (SDI), defined as (UTS-YS) * plastic strain, plotted as a function of grain size and h.c.p. ε-phase fraction for the TRIP HEA processed upon various processing conditions. The plot in Fig. 4a suggests that grain refinement in the TRIP HEAs leads to greater improvement in the SDI value than observed for the Fe20Mn20Co20Cr20Ni20 equiatomic reference HEA. Moreover, a non-TRIP Al0.1CoCrFeNi HEA, after subjecting it to a FSP, showed a lower SDI value compared to TRIP HEAs with and without FSP exposure. This clearly indicates that TRIP HEAs have superior work hardenability when compared to more stable single phase HEAs, and have a strong potential to overcome the inverse relationship between strength and ductility.

Nevertheless, one can envisage the broader scenario shown in schematic fashion in Fig. 4. Specifically, as the deformation energy, and accordingly the defect density, is increased, elastic deformation gives way to the generation of dislocations and their motion, then to deformation twinning, then phase transitions until finally in the extreme high strain (and/or high strain rate) regime, where amorphization can occur. The boundary between each mechanism can be loosely delineated by critical defect densities, which shift the free-energy barrier between different phases. The CrMnFeCoNi HEA has a very low stacking-fault energy, which favors defect accumulation during deformation since low stacking-fault energies lead to the dissociation of dislocations with a larger spacing between the partials; this, in turn, acts to severely inhibit the cross-slip of screw dislocations and consequently reduces the probability of dislocation annihilation.
